overview: Redis-Cluster style 16384 hash slots, a proxy tier routes requests, primaries replicate to replicas, gossip detects failures and promotes replicas.

estimation.assumption: Illustrative hot set: 10M keys at 1 KB/value.
estimation.calculation: 10,000,000 × 1 KB ≈ 10 GB payload; two copies ≈ 20 GB before overhead.
estimation.result: Metadata, fragmentation and failover headroom increase the memory budget.
estimation.implication: Partition memory across shards; size for a failed shard moving to survivors.

entityDetails.purpose: Disposable hot data with bounded staleness.
accessPatterns: GET by key; SET/DELETE by key; bulk warmup only with rate limits.
constraints: TTL and eviction can remove any entry. Cache failure must not become permanent data loss.

apiDetails.purpose: Read a key from its owning cache shard.
apiDetails.rationale: Client-ring or proxy routing chooses the shard. A miss causes the application, not the cache, to fetch the source of truth.
Hash key routing must be consistent for GET and SET. Never treat replication of cached data as a durable write guarantee.

steps.title: Users → LB → App servers → Cache routing proxies → Slot ownership metadata
steps.explanation: A proxy resolves the slot-owner map; application callers do not maintain the hash ring.

steps.title: Cache routing proxies → Cache cluster → Cache replicas
steps.explanation: Route GET/SET to the primary slot shard; replicate cached values to failover replicas.

steps.title: App servers → Cache routing proxies → Cache cluster
steps.explanation: A miss returns to the application and may occur after a slot move.

steps.title: App servers → Source of truth
steps.explanation: The application fetches the source record with a bounded concurrency budget.

steps.title: App servers → Cache routing proxies → Cache cluster
steps.explanation: Cache the result; avoid a retry loop when slot ownership changes.

failureCases.scenario: A cache shard dies or membership changes
failureCases.handling: Treat misses as recoverable; rebuild gradually with request coalescing and jittered TTLs. Bound source-of-truth load, and version membership to prevent inconsistent routing loops.

alternatives: Use a client-side ring when applications can share a versioned routing library. Use proxies/hash slots for simpler clients, accepting another hop and a separately scaled routing fleet.
